sections.title: Three verb forms: does, command, dictionary
body: A verb is an action word. The present tense says what happens now and normally ends in r: talar, köper, bor. Swedish uses the same present form for I study and I am studying: Jag pluggar. Never say Jag är pluggar.
The imperative is the command form: tala!, köp!, ring! It is the naked base. The infinitive is the dictionary form, often ending in a: tala, köpa, ringa. Two short exceptions are bo and må.
One important irregular verb is vara (be): är in the present and var! as a command. Compare Jag är trött, Jag vill vara pigg and Var glad! With kommer, the command loses one m: Kom!

examples.fi: Jag talar svenska. · Tala svenska! · Jag kan tala svenska.
examples.en: I speak Swedish. · Speak Swedish! · I can speak Swedish.

examples.fi: Jag köper bröd. · Köp bröd! · Jag vill köpa bröd.
examples.en: I buy bread. · Buy bread! · I want to buy bread.
examples.note: Köper loses er for the command and adds a for the infinitive.

examples.fi: Jag mår bra. · Må bra! · Jag vill må bättre.
examples.en: I feel well. · Be well! · I want to feel better.
examples.note: Må is a short infinitive exception.

examples.fi: Jag är glad. · Var glad! · Jag vill vara glad.
examples.en: I am happy. · Be happy! · I want to be happy.
examples.note: Vara changes to är in the present and var in a command.

sections.memoryTip: Present wears r. A command is naked. The dictionary form often ends in a.

sections.title: Help verbs open the door to an infinitive
body: Kan (can), vill (want), måste (must) and ska (will/plan to) are help verbs. The next verb uses the infinitive: kan tala, vill köpa, måste jobba, ska träna. Do not add r to that second verb.
Hinner means have enough time; orkar means have enough energy. They work the same way: Jag hinner komma. Jag orkar inte plugga. Vill ha is the normal way to say want something.

examples.fi: Jag kan sjunga, men jag kan inte dansa.
examples.en: I can sing, but I cannot dance.
examples.note: Both verbs after kan are infinitives.
Use vill ha for wanting a thing.

examples.fi: I morgon ska jag träffa Elin.
examples.en: Tomorrow I’m going to meet Elin.
examples.note: Ska marks a plan; träffa is infinitive.

examples.en: I have time to go to the shop.

sections.title: Inte comes after the first verb
body: Inte is the negation word: it makes a sentence negative. Put it after the first verb. With one verb: Jag simmar inte. With a help verb: Jag kan inte simma. Kan is first, so inte comes before the infinitive simma.
This rule also works with vill, ska, måste, hinner and orkar: Jag vill inte ha kaffe. Jag ska inte jobba. Jag orkar inte plugga.

sections.title: The verb stays second
body: A Swedish main sentence has one golden rule: the first verb is in position two. The first position can be the person: Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag. Or it can be a time: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

When time comes first, the subject moves after the verb. Count chunks, not single words: I dag is one first-position chunk. With a help verb: I morgon ska jag inte jobba. Ska is second, jag comes next, then inte.

examples.fi: Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag.
examples.en: My mother bakes a cake today.

examples.fi: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
examples.en: Today my mother bakes a cake.
examples.note: Time first, then verb, then subject.

examples.fi: Just nu kan jag inte plugga.
examples.note: Just nu is position one; kan is position two.

examples.fi: I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe varje dag.
examples.en: In Finland we drink a lot of coffee every day.

takeaways: Present tense usually ends in r; the command is the naked verb; the infinitive is the dictionary form.
After kan, vill, måste and ska, use the infinitive: Jag kan tala.
Put inte after the first verb: Jag kan inte komma.
A time phrase may come first, but the verb stays second: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
